A student is determining the focal length of a lens.

Fig. 3.1 shows the apparatus used.

![q3-series-3](assets/007-q3-series-3.jpg)

The student adjusts the position of the screen until a clearly focused image is formed on the screen.

The distance *v* on Fig. 3.1 is measured to be 5.80 cm.

(i) Fig. 3.1 is drawn 1/5<sup>th</sup> actual size.

Calculate *V*, the actual distance from the lens to the screen

*V* = ......................................................... [1]

(ii) With a clearly focused image formed on the screen, the actual distance from the centre of the lens to the illuminated object, *U* is 20.0 cm.

Calculate the focal length *f*<sub>*1*</sub> of the lens using the equation $f_{1} = \frac{U V}{( U + V )}$

*f*<sub>*1*</sub> = ......................................................... [2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Calculate *V*:

List the known quantities:

- Measured distance *v* = 5.80 cm
- Scale of drawing to actual size = 1/5<sup>th</sup>

Calculate the actual distance, *V*:

- $V=5\timesv=5\times5.8=29.0$ cm **[1 mark]**

** **

(ii) Calculate the focal length *f*<sub>*1*</sub> using the equation:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from lens to image,* V *= 29.0 cm
- Distance from lens to object, *U *= 20.0 cm

Substitute the known quantities into the equation for *f*<sub>*1*</sub>:

- $f_{1} = \frac{U V}{( U + V )}$
- $f_{1} = \frac{20 \times 29}{( 20 + 29 )}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate *f*<sub>*1*</sub>:

- *f*<sub>*1*</sub> = 11.83 cm = 11.8 cm (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This question requires no physics knowledge whatsoever! You just need to read and **follow the instructions**!*

parts.solution_md:
Calculate the average value *f*<sub>*A*</sub> of the focal length of the lens:

List the known quantities:

- Focal length 1,* f*<sub>*1*</sub> = 11.8 cm (from part (a) (ii))
- Focal length 2,* f*<sub>*2*</sub> = 12.2 cm

Obtain an equation for calculating the average focal length, *f*<sub>*A*</sub>:

- There are two measurements for focal length

  - The sum of the focal lengths must therefore be divided by 2
- So, $f_{A} = \frac{( f_{1} + f_{2} )}{2}$

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to calculate *f*<sub>*A*</sub>:

- $f_{A} = \frac{( 11.8 + 12.2 ) }{2}$
- *f*<sub>*A*</sub>* *= 12.0 cm **[1 mark]**

A person stands 2.0 m in front of a plane mirror and then takes one step back so that they are 3.0 m from the mirror.

What is the distance between the person and their image after they take a step back?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In a plane mirror, the image is formed the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it
- After stepping back, the person is 3.0 m in front of the mirror
- The image is therefore 3.0 m behind the mirror
- The distance between the person and their image is:

$\text{distance} = 3 . 0 + 3 . 0 = 6 . 0 \text{m}$

**A** is incorrect because 3.0 m is only the distance from the person to the mirror, not from the person to their image.

**B** is incorrect because this would be the distance between the person and their image at the original position (2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 m), before they stepped back.

**C** is incorrect because it adds the old distance to the new distance (2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 m).

An object is placed 9 cm in front of a thin converging lens. The scale diagram shows how the lens forms a real, inverted image.

![A ray diagram showing an object on the left side of a converging lens. Two rays are drawn from the top of the object: one passing through the centre of the lens undeviated, and one parallel to the principal axis refracting through the focal point on the other side. The image is formed where the rays meet, on the right side of the lens, inverted and smaller than the object. An arrow indicates that a large grid square is equal to 6.0 cm.](assets/038-a-ray-diagram-showing-an-object-on-the-left-side.png)

Which row gives the focal length of the lens and the distance of the image from the lens?

|   | focal length of lens / cm | distance of image from lens / cm |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 6.0 | 18.0 |
| **B** | 9.0 | 12.0 |
| **C** | 12.0 | 9.0 |
| **D** | 18.0 | 6.0 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The scale on the diagram shows that 1 large grid square represents a distance of $6 . 0 \text{cm}$
- The focal length is the distance between the centre of the lens and the principal focus
- A ray that travels parallel to the principal axis refracts and passes through the principal focus on the other side of the lens
- On the diagram, the parallel ray crosses the principal axis exactly 1 large square from the centre of the lens, so the focal length is:

$\mathrm{focal} \mathrm{length}=1\times6.0=6.0\text{cm}$

- The image is formed where the two rays meet
- The horizontal distance from the centre of the lens to the image is 3 large squares, so the distance of the image from the lens is:

$\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{image}=3\times6.0=18.0\text{cm}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the two standard rays used to locate an image for a converging lens. A ray travelling through the optical centre of the lens does not change direction. A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis will refract and pass through the principal focus. Identifying these rays will help you locate the principal focus and measure the focal length accurately.

parts.problem_md:
A student uses a thin converging lens with a focal length $f$ of $10 \text{cm}$ to produce a real, inverted, and magnified image of an object.

Where must the object be placed?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The characteristics of an image formed by a converging lens depend on the position of the object relative to the focal length $f$
- To produce a real, inverted, and magnified image, the object must be placed between $f$ and $2f$
- In this case, $f=10\text{cm}$ and $2f=20\text{cm}$, so the object distance must be between $10\text{cm}$ and $20\text{cm}$
- Therefore, the distance must be $15\text{cm}$ from the lens, which is option **C**

**A** is incorrect because placing the object closer than $f$ ($5 \text{cm}$) would produce a virtual, upright, and magnified image.

**B** is incorrect because when an object is exactly at the focal point $f$ ($10 \text{cm}$), the rays emerge parallel and no image is formed.

**D** is incorrect because when the object is beyond $2 f$ ($25 \text{cm}$), the image formed is real and inverted, but it is diminished (smaller).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the key positions for a converging lens:
> 
> - objects placed closer than $f$ give virtual, upright, magnified images
> - objects between $f$ and $2 f$ give real, inverted, magnified images

parts.problem_md:
The diagram shows a light ray incident on the boundary between a glass block and air at point O.

![A light ray enters the curved edge of a semicircular glass block. The ray hits the midpoint of the straight edge at O, and 4 possible refraction paths are shown, labelled A, B, C, D.](assets/039-a-light-ray-enters-the-curved-edge-of-a-semicirc.png)

The angle of incidence $i$ is $25 ^{\circ}$. The critical angle for the glass is $42 ^{\circ}$.

Which path does the light ray take after point O?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When light travels from an optically denser medium (glass) to a less dense medium (air), it refracts away from the normal
- Total internal reflection only occurs if the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
- In this case, the angle of incidence ($25 ^{\circ}$) is less than the critical angle ($42 ^{\circ}$), so the light will refract out into the air
- Path **B** shows the ray bending away from the normal as it enters the air

**A** is incorrect as it shows the ray bending towards the normal.

**C** is incorrect as the light only travels along the boundary if the angle of incidence is exactly $42 ^{\circ}$.

**D** is incorrect as total internal reflection only occurs if the angle of incidence is greater than $42 ^{\circ}$.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the key rule: when light passes from a denser to a less dense medium, it bends away from the normal. Always compare the angle of incidence to the critical angle first:
> 
> - if the angle of incidence is less than the critical angle $( i < c )$, refraction occurs
> - if the angle of incidence is equal to the critical angle $( i = c )$, light travels along the boundary
> - if the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle $( i > c )$, total internal reflection occurs

parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The refractive index of a material is given by:

$\text{refractive} \text{index} = \frac{ \text{sin} ( \text{angle} of \text{incidence} ) }{ \text{sin} ( \text{angle} of \text{refraction} ) } or \mathrm{n} = \frac{ \text{sin} \mathrm{i} }{ \text{sin} \mathrm{r} }$

- These angles must be measured from the normal, the dotted line at right angles to the surface.
- The angle of incidence (the incoming ray) is 90°− 50° = 40°
- The angle of refraction is 40°
- This gives the calculation for the refractive index *n* as: $n=\frac{\mathrm{sin}40^{\circ}}{\mathrm{sin}25^{\circ}}$

parts.problem_md:
Which diagram shows the dispersion of white light by a glass prism?

![diagram](assets/041-diagram.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The colours in white light will refract at different angles at every boundary, because they have different frequencies and wavelengths
- The spreading of white light into its component colours is called dispersion
- The first boundary causes the white light to disperse into its different colours
- The second boundary causes further dispersion of the colours
- Violet light refracts through a greater angle than red light

**A** is incorrect as the white light is not dispersing at the first boundary.

**C** is incorrect as the violet light is refracting in the wrong direction.

**D** is incorrect as the violet light is not refracting at the second boundary.

** **An object O is placed at point P near to a thin converging lens. The diagram shows three rays from the top of O passing through the lens. Each point F is one focal length from the centre of the lens. Each point 2F is two focal lengths from the centre of the lens.

![image](assets/042-image.png)

The object O is moved to point Q on the diagram.

Which type of image is produced when the object O is at point Q?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- For a converging lens, an object placed further than one focal length F will always produce an inverted image

  - Therefore, options **C** and **D** can be eliminated
- The closer the object is placed to the lens, the larger the size of the image

  - Therefore, the image produced when the object is at point Q will be inverted and enlarged compared to when the object is at point P

The difficult part of the question is ignoring the rays drawn on the diagram for the object at point P, as the question asks you to move it to point Q. The rays shown give an inverted image that is diminished (smaller), but this is not what the question asks about.

To find the properties of the image you can draw a new object at point Q and then draw two rays from the tip of the object. One should pass through the centre of the lens and one should travel parallel to the optical axis up to the lens and then through focal point F, as shown by the red rays in the diagram. The image is formed where these two lines cross.

![image](assets/043-image.png)

A student draws a diagram to show the directions of a light ray reflecting off a plane mirror.

![image](assets/044-image.png)

What are the correct terms for the lines drawn?

|   | **normal** | **incident ray** | **reflected ray** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| **B** | 1 | 3 | 2 |
| **C** | 2 | 1 | 3 |
| **D** | 2 | 3 | 1 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The normal is a line at right angles to a surface, this is line 2 in the diagram

  - Therefore options **A** and **B** are eliminated
- An incident ray is the ray approaching the surface. This is line 1 in the diagram
- A reflected ray is a line leaving a surface. This is line 3 in the diagram

The arrow on a ray shows the direction of travel. You should use this to see which way the light is going, and this will make it easy to identify the incident ray and other rays.

parts.problem_md:
An object is placed in front of a converging lens. The lens has a focal length f.

In which labelled position should the object be placed in order to produce a real image that is smaller than the object?

![Diagram of four arrows labelled A to D placed on a horizontal line showing distance from a convex lens, indicating focal length f and 2f.](assets/045-diagram-of-four-arrows-labelled-a-to-d-placed-on.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A because:**

- A real image is one formed by the convergence of rays of light and can be projected onto a screen

  - In this case, since the object is on the left of the lens, the projected image would be on the right of the lens
- To produce a real image that is smaller than the object, the object should be placed further than 2*f*

**B** & **C** are incorrect because an object placed at *f*, or between *f* and 2*f*, would produce a real image that is larger than the object

**D** is incorrect because an object placed closer than f would produce a virtual image that is larger than the object

parts.problem_md:
**Extended Tier Only**

The speed of light in air is 3.0 $\times$ 10<sup>8  </sup>m/s.

The critical angle for light in a transparent plastic material placed in air is 37°.

What is the speed of light in the plastic material?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A because:**

- The refractive index of the material is related to the critical angle by

$n=\frac{1}{sinc}=\frac{1}{sin37}=1.66$

- The speed of light in a plastic material can be found using refractive index

$n=\frac{speedoflightinair}{speedoflightinmaterial}$

- Therefore, the speed of light in the plastic material is

$speedoflightinmaterial=\frac{speedoflightinair}{n}$

$speedoflightinmaterial=\frac{3.0\times10^{8}}{1.66}=1.81\times10^{8}$ m/s

- This is option** A**

parts.problem_md:
The critical angle for the glass is 42°.

Calculate the refractive index of the glass.

Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the refractive index of the glass:

- Recall the equation for critical angle:

$\mathrm{sin}c=\frac{1}{n}$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange for $n$ and calculate:

$n=\frac{1}{\mathrm{sin}42^{\circ}}$

$n=$ $1.49$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct rearrangement **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $\mathrm{sin}c=\frac{1}{n}$ **OR** $n=\frac{1}{\mathrm{sin}c}$ **OR** $n=\frac{1}{\mathrm{sin}42^{\circ}}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct answer of $1.49$
> 
> - Accept any value that rounds to 1.5
> 
> Working must be shown to gain both marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating refractive index, remember that the refractive index of air is 1, so for materials such as glass or plastic, if your answer is less than 1, you have the formula inverted.

Always check whether the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle before deciding if the ray reflects or refracts.
> 
> If you draw the ray refracting out through the straight edge, you will score zero. Remember: the angle of reflection must equal the angle of incidence, and a ray hitting a curved surface along the normal will pass straight through without bending.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A student investigates the refraction of light through a rectangular glass block. Fig. 3.1 shows the student's ray-trace sheet.

A rectangular outline labelled ABCD. Side AB is the top surface. A point S is marked on AB. Below CD there are two points P3 and P4, and an eye symbol in the bottom right corner, indicating perspective.

On Fig. 3.1, draw a normal NL to the side AB of the block at the point S. Continue the normal so that it passes through side CD of the block.

The student observes the images of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ through the side **CD **of the block. They place two more pins, $P_{3}$ and $P_{4}$, so that they appear to be in a straight line with the images. Fig. 3.1 shows the positions of $P_{3}$ and $P_{4}$.

- Draw a line joining $P_{3}$ and $P_{4}$. Continue the line until it meets the normal **NL**.
- Label the point **T** where the line meets side **CD**. Draw the line **ST**.
- Measure the angle $r$ between **ST** and the normal.
parts.solution_md:
Draw a line joining $P_{3}$ and $P_{4}$ and the line **ST**:

![Straight line drawn from the eye in the bottom right corner to the normal line NL passing through points P3, P4, and T. A straight line is also drawn between point S on side AB and point T on side CD.](assets/080-straight-line-drawn-from-the-eye-in-the-bottom-r.png)

**[2 marks]**

Measure the angle $r$ between **ST** and the normal:

![A protractor at point S showing a 25 degree angle between ST and the normal NL.](assets/081-a-protractor-at-point-s-showing-a-25-degree-angl.png)

angle of refraction, $r=25^{\circ}$

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for drawing a straight line through $P_{3}$ and $P_{4}$ extended to meet the normal **NL**
> 
> 1 mark for labelling point **T** on **CD** and drawing line **ST**
> 
> 1 mark for measuring the angle of refraction $r=25^{\circ}$ ($\pm 1 ^{\circ}$)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When drawing lines through pins, always use a ruler to ensure the line is perfectly straight. Make sure your line is thin and clearly visible. For measuring angles, place the protractor carefully with its centre exactly on the point where the ray meets the normal, and read the scale accurately. Remember that the angle of refraction is measured from the normal, not from the surface.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A student investigates the refraction of light through a rectangular glass block.

Draw a line **RS** at an angle [i = 40°] to the normal, above **AB** and to the left of the normal.

The student plans to take more sets of readings to investigate the relationship between $i$ and $r$.

(i) Suggest other suitable values of angle $i$ that the student could use.

[2]

(ii) Suggest how the student could improve the experiment to check the reliability of their results.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Other suitable values of angle $i$ that the student could use:

20°, 30°, 50°, 60°

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for suggesting at least 3 extra values of angle $i$ which are all less than 90°.
> 
> 1 mark for a range of values spread over at least 30°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (ii) To check the reliability of their results, the student could:
> 
> - Repeat the experiment with the ray entering from the opposite side **AND** Take repeat readings and calculate a mean for each angle **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When suggesting values for angles in optics experiments, always ensure your values are physically possible (i.e. less than 90° for angles of incidence). Spreading your values over a wide range helps to establish a clear relationship between variables. For reliability, remember that repeating measurements and calculating means is a standard technique to reduce the effect of random errors.

![figure](assets/082-figure.png)

On Fig. 7.1, continue the path of each ray beyond the lens as far as the screen.
parts.solution_md:
The completed paths of each ray after passing through the lens are as follows:

![Diagram of a convex lens showing parallel light rays converging at focal point F1 on the principal axis, with labels for F1, F2, and screen.](assets/083-diagram-of-a-convex-lens-showing-parallel-light-.png)

- The two rays drawn are refracted towards the principal axis; **[1 mark]**
- The two rays pass through F<sub>1</sub> (one of the lens’s focal points); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rays must be drawn with a ruler, so that they are straight. You should use small arrows to show the direction of travel. Make sure that there are no gaps in the lines.

parts.problem_md:
**Extended Tier Only**

Fig. 7.1 is a full-scale diagram of a small nail N in front of a thin converging lens. The line L represents the lens.

![Graph paper with axes labelled X and Y. A vertical line L is shown along the Y-axis, with a small perpendicular line N. Scale marked as 1.0 cm intervals.](assets/084-graph-paper-with-axes-labelled-x-and-y-a-vertica.png)

The focal length of the lens is 3.0 cm.

Rays of light, parallel to XY, are travelling towards the lens.

Describe what happens to the light after it passes through the lens.
parts.solution_md:
When the light passes through the converging lens:

- (All the) light rays meet / focus / intersect (at a point); **[1 mark]**
- (All the) light rays travel towards a point; **[1 mark]**
- The light rays then diverge / spread out (from that point) **OR**
- The point of convergence is on XY / at F / the focal point / principal focus / 3.0 cm from the lens; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

Fig. 7.1 is a full-scale diagram of a small nail N in front of a thin converging lens. The line L represents the lens. The focal length of the lens is 3.0 cm. Rays of light, parallel to XY, are travelling towards the lens. On Fig. 7.1, the two principal focuses of the lens are marked on XY 3.0 cm from the centre of the lens, one point on the left and one point on the right of the lens, each labelled F. The small nail N, of height 1.2 cm, is positioned 2.0 cm to the left of the lens.

**Extended Tier Only**

The small nail N, of height 1.2 cm, is positioned 2.0 cm to the left of the lens.

(i) By drawing on Fig. 7.1, find the position of the image I of N and add image I to the diagram.

[3]

(ii) State and explain whether I is a real or a virtual image.

[1]

(iii)** **State the name given to a lens when it is used in this way.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The image I of N can be shown on Fig 7.1 as follows:

![Graph showing light rays on a grid with two focal points labelled F, arrows indicating direction, and measurements in centimetres.](assets/086-graph-showing-light-rays-on-a-grid-with-two-foca.png)

Rays drawn from the tip of nail N:

Any **two **from:

- A ray (that seems to come) from left-hand principal focus **AND **emerges from lens paraxially (parallel to XY); **[1 mark]**
- A paraxial ray to lens **AND **then towards right-hand principal focus; **[1 mark]**
- A ray towards / through the centre of lens;** ****[1 mark]**

Plus one mark for determining the location of image I:

- Two rays traced back to the intersection **AND **a** **line drawn from the intersection to axis labelled I; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Image I is

- <u>Virtual</u>

**AND **any **one **from:

- Light / rays do not pass through I; **[1 mark]**
- Light / rays only seem to come from I; **[1 mark]**
- I is produced by diverging rays;** [1 mark]**
- (Real) rays do not meet / intersect; **[1 mark]**

(iii) This type of lens can be used as a

- Magnifying glass; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

The water waves travel from deep water into shallow water. The water waves have a lower speed in the shallow water.

Fig. 7.2 shows wavefronts for the waves in deep water to the left of the boundary.
